pedagogy.summary: At 7-8, using structure extends place value to three digits (adding hundreds changes only the hundreds digit), turns the multiplication/division link into a fact-deriving tool (6×4=24 gives 4×6, 24÷4 and 24÷6), and makes shape classification property-based (sort by number of sides, right angles, parallel lines rather than by look). The teaching aim is a habit: before computing or naming, ask 'what do I already know that this is like?' CCSS MP7 marks this as the run-up to the distributive property (7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3) and to reasoning about geometric figures by their structure.
bestPractices: Use a single array to show a whole fact family at once (6 rows of 4) so 6×4, 4×6, 24÷4 and 24÷6 are read off one structure, not learned as four separate facts
Use a three-digit place-value machine / arrow cards and predict-then-check which column moves when adding 100, 10 or 1
Classify shapes with property checklists and overlapping sets (sides, right angles, parallel pairs) so classification survives rotation and odd examples
Ask 'which fact that you already know helps here?' to build the transfer habit rather than fresh computation
keyRepresentations: Rectangular array / area model for the multiplication-division fact family
Three-digit place-value apparatus and arrow cards
Property checklists and Venn-style overlapping shape sets
Distributive splits (7×8 as 7×5 + 7×3) shown on a partitioned array
commonMisconceptions: Treats multiplication and division as unrelated, recomputing 24÷4 from scratch despite knowing 6×4
When adding 100 to a three-digit number, changes the wrong column or mis-carries
Classifies shapes by orientation/appearance (a rotated square becomes a 'diamond'; only a 'pointing-up' triangle is a triangle)
Thinks a derived fact must be checked by counting because facts feel separate rather than connected

learn.summary: For ages 7-8, build the habit of looking for structure before computing or naming: ask 'what do I already know that this is like?' Three strands: (1) read a whole multiplication/division fact family off one array (6×4, 4×6, 24÷4, 24÷6 from the same 6 rows of 4); (2) use three-digit place value so adding 100/10/1 changes only the matching column, barring a carry into the next place; (3) classify shapes by properties (sides, right angles, parallel pairs) so the classification survives rotation. This is the run-up to the distributive property (7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3) and to reasoning about figures by structure.

activities.title: One array, four facts
feedback: If the child pauses to count or skip-count for the divisions, return to the one array and physically read all four facts from it (rows, columns, sharing, grouping) so the single structure is seen to hold them all; name division as undoing multiplication.
If they treat 24÷4 as unrelated to 6×4, cover a factor on the array they just built and ask 'how many fours are hidden here?' so the quotient is read, not recalculated.
Probe scaling: 'you knew 6×4 — does that also help with 6×8, or 60×4? how?' to check the structural link transfers.
Counterexample check: 'division undoes multiplication — so does 24÷5 come out as neat as 24÷4? why not?' to test understanding beyond the slogan.
activities.rationale: A single manipulable array makes the shared structure of a fact family visible as the child acts, supporting the deriving habit rather than four separately memorised facts; well-chosen representations such as arrays expose structure and can later be faded.
sourceClaims: Teaching should help pupils recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships, using well-chosen representations (e.g. arrays, place-value apparatus) that expose structure and are then faded
Students using structure see e.g. 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3 (distributive property) and recognise significant structure in figures — the run-up to reasoning by structure rather than recomputation
learnerActions: Lay out 24 counters as 6 rows of 4 and state the multiplication it shows (6×4=24).
Rotate the whole array a quarter turn and read it again as 4 rows of 6; say why 6×4 and 4×6 are the same 24 dots seen two ways.
Cover one factor: with 24 shared into 4 rows, read off how many are in each row (6) to get 24÷4; then read 24÷6 the same way.
Say in your own words how knowing 6×4=24 means you already know 24÷4 and 24÷6 without counting.
Try a second fact family (e.g. 5 rows of 3) and derive all four facts from the single array.
activities.intendedInsight: One rectangular array holds a whole fact family; multiplication and division are the same structure read different ways, so a known product gives the related quotients without recomputing.

activities.title: Partition to derive a harder product
feedback: If the parts don't recombine, re-count each sub-array (7×5 and 7×3) separately before adding, and check the split covers all 8 columns with none missing.
Audit the arithmetic together: 35+21=56; if a child suggests another total, recount one part on the array rather than accepting the number.
Ask them to split the same product a second way (e.g. 7×4 + 7×4, where each part is 28 and the total is again 56) and confirm it reaches the same total, reinforcing that the whole is conserved.
activities.rationale: Showing the distributive split on a partitioned array connects the fact-deriving habit to standard structural reasoning named in the practice standards.
sourceClaims: Students using structure see e.g. 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3 (distributive property) and recognise significant structure in figures — the run-up to reasoning by structure rather than recomputation
learnerActions: Take a product you don't know by heart, e.g. 7×8, and lay it as 7 rows of 8.
Split the 8 columns into 5 and 3, drawing a line through the array.
Work out the two easier parts (7×5=35 and 7×3=21) and add them (35+21=56).
State the rule you used: 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3, then try splitting a different product your own way.
activities.intendedInsight: A large product can be built from easier known products by partitioning the array — this is the distributive property seen concretely.

activities.title: Predict which column moves
feedback: If the child names or alters the wrong column when adding 100, predict-then-check on the place-value machine and watch only the hundreds count move.
If a carry occurs (e.g. adding 100 to 970 → 1070), treat it explicitly: the hundreds column fills and rolls into thousands — note this is still the hundreds place acting, not a random digit changing.
Probe directly: 'which digit changes when I add 100 to 470, and which stay the same? why those?'
activities.rationale: Predict-then-check with place-value apparatus makes the column structure something the child reasons about rather than a procedure to copy; such representations expose structure and can be faded.
sourceClaims: Teaching should help pupils recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships, using well-chosen representations (e.g. arrays, place-value apparatus) that expose structure and are then faded
learnerActions: Using a three-digit place-value apparatus or arrow cards, build a number such as 253 (or 470).
Before adding, predict out loud which digit will change and which will stay the same when you add 100.
Add one hundred-flat (or spin the +100 wheel) and check: for 253 and 470 only the hundreds count moves, with no carry.

Repeat for +10 and +1, each time predicting first, then stating why only that one column changed (true for 253 or 470; if the column being added to holds a 9, notice that a carry also changes the next place).
activities.intendedInsight: Place value is structured by columns; adding 100 changes only the hundreds, 10 only the tens, and 1 only the ones, unless the addition causes a carry into the next place (e.g. 259+1=260, 295+10=305, 970+100=1070).

activities.title: Classify by properties, not by how it looks
feedback: If the child says a rotated square is a 'diamond' and no longer a square, or that only a point-up triangle is a triangle, run the property checklist while rotating the shape so they see the properties are unchanged by orientation.
If they justify by appearance, ask 'count the sides and right angles — did any change when it tilted?' to redirect to properties.
Include odd and rotated examples deliberately so classification does not depend on a standard pose.
activities.rationale: Property checklists and overlapping sets make classification depend on structure rather than orientation, addressing the common misconception that a rotated square becomes a 'diamond' and is no longer a square; recognising significant structure in figures is the aimed-for habit.
sourceClaims: Students using structure see e.g. 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3 (distributive property) and recognise significant structure in figures — the run-up to reasoning by structure rather than recomputation
learnerActions: Pick a shape and run a property checklist: count the sides, mark the right angles, find any parallel pairs.
Classify it from the checklist (e.g. square: 4 equal sides, 4 right angles, 2 pairs of parallel sides — also a rectangle).
Rotate the shape 45° and re-run the checklist; confirm the same properties, so the classification does not change.
Sort several shapes into overlapping sets (e.g. 'has a right angle', 'has parallel sides') and place a rotated square and an upside-down triangle correctly.
Justify one classification aloud by citing properties, not orientation.
activities.intendedInsight: A shape's class comes from its properties (sides, angles, parallel lines), which stay the same under rotation — a tilted square is still a square; calling it a 'diamond' does not make it a different shape (a square is also a special rhombus).

constraints: The teaching aim is the transfer habit 'which fact that I already know helps here?' — reaching the right numbers is not enough; the child should explain why one fact yields the others.

A fixed reference diagram of a fact family or distributive split can annotate and explain, but cannot be rotated or re-covered by the learner; a manipulable array lets the child test that a turned array re-reads and that covering a factor reveals a quotient. Use static diagrams as support, not as the sole route to the deriving habit.

Matching or derive-the-answer tasks (from 6×4=24, give 24÷6) can check whether facts are treated as connected, but a correct answer may be a recomputed one; always pair with 'which known fact did you use?' to distinguish deriving from recalculating.

Carrying is an exception to 'only one column changes': when adding 100/10/1 causes a carry, the named column fills and rolls into the next place. Address this explicitly rather than teaching 'the other columns never change'.

Fact families and three-digit place value are quantitative; 2D shape classification by property needs the 2D figure and its properties. These do not require 3D models, though a 3D context is not forbidden where genuinely useful.

Optional interaction examples (tap to highlight 6×4, rotate the array to read 4×6, cover a factor to reveal a division, a predict-then-check place-value wheel, live recolouring of a checklist while rotating a shape) make the mechanism concrete; they are illustrative, not mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support general principles rather than proving any specific task was tested.

The original claimed adding 100 'only changes the hundreds digit'; this holds except when a carry occurs. The summary, Activity 3 and the constraints now qualify the generalisation, and the child predicts and checks, so it is not taught as absolute.

The original artefact notes asserted a dialogue 'lacks the array and columns the child needs' and that these topics 'do not need 3D'. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established necessity claims; softened to scoped affordances/limits in constraints.
Arithmetic self-audit: 6×4=24; 24÷4=6; 24÷6=4; 5×3=15; 7×5=35, 7×3=21, 35+21=56 (=7×8); alternative split 7×4+7×4 = 28+28 = 56; 970+100=1070. All checked and consistent as used in activities.
Source claims as written describe general guidance (recognise/use structure; use and fade representations) and do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity of any particular artefact type.

probeDeeper: Ask 'you knew 6×4 — does knowing 6×4 also help with 6×8, or 60×4? how?' to test whether the structural link scales to new facts
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'you said division undoes multiplication — so does 24÷5 come out as neat as 24÷4? why not?' to check the child understands the relationship, not a slogan
Ask 'which digit changes when I add 100 to 470, and which stay the same? why those?' to probe the place-value structure directly
Rotate a square 45° and ask 'is it still a square? how can you be sure?' — a structural thinker checks sides and angles, not the tilt
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child deriving all three from the one fact and explaining the link: 4×6 is the same array turned round; 24÷4 asks how many fours in 24 (six), 24÷6 asks how many sixes (four) — division undoes the multiplication.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats multiplication and division as unrelated operations, recomputing 24÷4 from scratch despite just stating 6×4=24
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to one array and physically read all four facts from it (rows, columns, sharing, grouping) so the single structure is seen to hold them all; name division as undoing multiplication
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child pauses to count or skip-count for the divisions rather than reading them off the known fact

errorPatterns.pattern: When adding hundreds, changes the wrong column (253+100 alters tens or ones) because three-digit place-value structure is insecure
errorPatterns.nextMove: Predict-then-check on a three-digit place-value machine; add one hundred-flat and watch only the hundreds count move
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked which digit changes when adding 100 to a three-digit number, the child names or alters the wrong column

errorPatterns.pattern: Classifies shapes by orientation or appearance — a rotated square becomes a 'diamond', or only checks how it looks rather than its sides/angles/parallel lines
errorPatterns.nextMove: Run a property checklist (sides, right angles, parallel lines) while rotating the shape so the child sees the properties are unchanged by orientation
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked to justify a classification, the child cites how the shape looks or which way it points rather than counting sides/right angles/parallel pairs

responseLevels.gap: Recomputes divisions from scratch, mis-places the changing digit when adding hundreds, and classifies shapes by look; each task handled in isolation
responseLevels.full: Reads all four facts off the one array and explains the inverse relationship, predicts and justifies which digit changes, and classifies by properties despite rotation — and reuses 'what do I already know that this is like?' on new problems unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Derives the related facts or names the right column/property when prompted, but cannot clearly explain why one fact gives the others or reverts to counting under pressure

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You know that 6 × 4 = 24. Without counting anything out, what does that tell you about 4 × 6, and about 24 ÷ 4 and 24 ÷ 6? How does the one fact give you the others?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reaching the numbers is easy; the discriminating content is the EXPLANATION of why one fact yields the others. A child using structure narrates the array/inverse relationship; a child without it treats each as a separate fact to recompute or recall, or gets the divisions but cannot say why they follow.
